phonemes.desc: Short open vowel; the alef ꜣ in the spelling colours or lengthens the vowel but is not pronounced as a separate consonant here.
Voiced postalveolar affricate [d͡ʒ], the conventional Egyptological reading of ḏ (d-with-line-below, U+1E0F); Coptic evidence later points to a /t/ reflex, as in Coptic ⲟⲩⲱⲧ 'green'.
Long close front vowel in the final syllable.
Voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the final -t is the feminine marker.

pronunciation.approximation: 'WAD-jeet' — start like 'wad', then 'jeet' with a long 'ee' and a crisp final t. The middle consonant may also be pronounced as a sharp emphatic 't' in stricter reconstructions.

pronunciation.note: The name Wꜣḏyt derives from the Egyptian word for 'green/blue' (wꜣḏ), recorded in Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache I, 263–268. Hieroglyphs write only the consonants w-ꜣ-ḏ-y-t; the vowels are uncertain. The ꜣ functions as a vowel carrier or glottal onset, and the ḏ (palatal/ejective in earlier Egyptian, later merging toward /t/) is represented in PUNICODEX by the registrable d-with-line-below (U+1E0F). Because DNS registries vary in their acceptance of combining marks, the practical fallback is 'wadjet'. This is a Tier 1 restoration — the ꜣ and ḏ are distinctive letters the ASCII form loses. Sources: Allen, Middle Egyptian (2014); Faulkner, A Concise Dictionary of Middle Egyptian, s.v. wꜣḏ; Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache I, s.v. wꜣḏ; Hoch, Semitic Words in Egyptian Texts (1994), on Egyptian ḏ in Semitic transcriptions.

domains.title: The Cobra Crown of Lower Egypt
domains.subtitle: Protection, Sovereignty, and the Living Eye
domains.lead:
Wꜣḏyt is the cobra that rears from the king's brow. Patron goddess of Lower Egypt and protector of the living pharaoh, she strikes at enemies with flame and venom while shielding the land with her hooded vigilance. Her name means 'the green one' or 'the flourishing one,' the color of new growth, of malachite, and of the papyrus-filled Delta.

She is one half of the nbty, the Two Ladies, paired with Nekhbet the vulture of Upper Egypt. Together they bind the Two Lands into one kingship. Without Wadjet, the red crown has no fangs; without her, the uraeus is only jewelry.

mythology.lead: Wadjet's mythology is woven into kingship from the first dynasties, present more as an institution than a protagonist. She has no single epic cycle; she has a thousand crowns, amulets, and royal names — and her stories cluster around four poles: the Two Ladies, the divine child, the wandering Eye, and the Delta oracle at Buto.

myths.title: The Two Ladies
myths.text: From the unification of the Two Lands, the cobra stood beside the vulture over every royal name: Wadjet of the Delta and Nekhbet of Elkab together were the nbty, the Two Ladies, and their pairing was the political theology of Egypt — two lands, two crowns, one body wearing both. On the Narmer Palette (Cairo JE 32169), the king of the First Dynasty already processes beneath the standards of his protectors, and the serekhs of his successors frame the royal name with the two beasts. By the reign of King Den the pair had entered the titulary itself as the title nbty, 'He of the Two Ladies' — the first element of the fivefold royal protocol. Every coronation oath for three thousand years was thus sworn in her presence, on the brow. The myth is a constitution written as heraldry: sovereignty is legitimate only when north and south, vulture and cobra, consent to share a single head.

myths.title: Nurse of the Divine Child
myths.text: In the Delta marshes, when Isis hid the infant Horus from Seth among the papyrus thickets of Chemmis, the snakes of the goddess stood guard. Wadjet is the serpent of the thicket — hood spread over the nursing god, flame ready for any scavenging demon. The protection was theologically exact: Horus was the king, so the Delta goddess guarded in myth what her uraeus guarded in fact, the brow of every living pharaoh, 'the nursling of Wadjet'. The scene's most beloved monument is the Metternich Stela and its kin, the Horus cippi of the Late Period (c. 360 BCE): on them the child-god, stung by scorpions in the reeds, is healed by his mother while the surrounding deities — Wadjet among them — contract to shield the cippi's owner from every crawling thing. The myth taught an Egyptian peasant of any century the same lesson the crown taught the court: in the reeds, as on the throne, survival depends on a serpent who has chosen you.

myths.title: The Distant Goddess Returns
myths.text: Like Sekhmet, Tefnut, and Hathor, Wadjet can act as the solar Eye that departs in rage and must be coaxed home. The cycle is set out in the great commentaries on Book of the Dead spell 17: the Eye of Horus is struck down and scattered — by Seth in one telling — and Thoth gathers and restores it, the sound, whole, 'wedjat' eye; restored, it burns from the king's brow as the uraeus, the healed eye that has become a weapon. When the Eye wanders far south as the Distant Goddess, the land withers; when it returns, the Delta greens. For Wadjet the return is literal: her name means 'the green one', and her homecoming is the inundation's fresh silt spreading over the fields. The theology binds protection to growth in a single image: the same eye that was broken and made whole now makes the land whole, and the cobra on the crown is the scar tissue of the cosmos — injury, restored, promoted to sentry.

myths.title: Buto and the Oracle
myths.text: Her ancient cult center was Pe-Dep — the twin towns of Pe and Dep in the western Delta, Greek Buto — where she was worshipped in a temple famed as an oracle; Herodotus (2.59) counts Buto among Egypt's great oracular shrines, and (2.63) describes its sanctuary with the respect he reserves for the old and uncanny. There, in the reeds of the deepest Delta, Egyptian theology placed the primordial mound where creation began and where Isis nursed Horus — Buto was the wet nurse of the world. Greek visitors, hearing that this goddess guarded a divine child in a marsh, identified her city with Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, two other children hidden in reeds — an interpretatio the sources themselves found almost too neat. Excavations at Tell el-Fara'in have uncovered the temple's Late Period and Ptolemaic remains above occupation layers reaching back into prehistory, confirming what the priests always claimed: Buto was old before Egypt had a name for old.

lore.syncretism: Wadjet is inseparable from Nekhbet; the Two Ladies form a single institution of kingship. She merges with the solar eye and therefore with Hathor, Sekhmet, Tefnut, and Mut as the goddess who departs and returns. Her uraeus becomes the emblem of Egyptian royalty and passes into Hellenistic and Roman iconography as the serpent of sovereign power — Cleopatra's asp was, in the end, only the oldest member of her household staff. Greek writers called her Buto and identified her city with Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis, because both were protectors of divine children in reedy marshes. The Coptic name ⲟⲩⲱⲧ/ⲟⲩⲉⲧ preserves the root meaning 'green', the last breath of the word after the temples closed.
lore.culturalLegacy: The uraeus never went out of style. It survives on crowns and crests from Ptolemaic queens to modern heraldry, a shorthand for divine authority and national unity. The Eye of Horus — the Wedjat — remains one of the most popular protective amulets in the world, worn as jewelry and tattooed as a symbol of wholeness. In modern Egyptology, Wadjet is a reminder that the king's power was not abstract: it was a rearing cobra with real flames. And her color lives on wherever the Delta still floods — in a word, wadjet, 'the green one', remains the oldest description of Egypt's renewal that anyone still speaks.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Wadjet is vigilance made beautiful. The cobra on the crown is not decoration; it is the land's immune system, a living warning that the king is protected by something older and faster than any army. She asks us to notice how much sovereignty depends on the threat of defense, and how much protection depends on patience.

In her green aspect, Wadjet is also the color of return. The Delta after the inundation, the papyrus after the flood, the eye restored after injury — all these are her signatures. She teaches that protection and growth are not opposites. The same cobra that strikes the intruder also shelters the nest. To wear her image is to claim that the land and its people are worth both tenderness and venom.

lore.archaeology: Wadjet's earliest evidence appears on the Narmer Palette (Cairo JE 32169) and in the royal serekh of the First Dynasty, where the cobra guards the king's name. Her temple at Buto (Tell el-Fara'in / Pe-Dep) in the western Delta has been excavated by German and Egyptian teams, revealing Late Period and Ptolemaic remains above occupation layers reaching back into prehistory. Uraei in gold, faience, and stone crown royal statues and coffins from the Old Kingdom to the Ptolemaic era. Wedjat-eye amulets are found in virtually every Egyptian burial context, and the Metternich Stela (c. 360 BCE, now in the Metropolitan Museum) preserves the fullest monument of her child-guardian cycle.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written w-ꜣ-ḏ-y-t, derived from the root wꜣḏ, 'green, blue, fresh, flourishing.' The ꜣ functions as a vowel carrier or glottal onset; the ḏ represents a palatal/ejective consonant in earlier Egyptian, later merging with /t/, represented in PuniCodex by d-with-line-below (U+1E0F). Coptic preserves the root as ⲟⲩⲱⲧ/ⲟⲩⲉⲧ (ouōt/ouət), 'green.' The registrable Wꜣḏyt restores the historic consonants while leaving the vowels, as always, to Egyptological reconstruction.
